claim: Federal law separately defines wire, oral, and electronic communications and interception; classification must precede analysis
limitations: Classification and contemporaneous acquisition remain fact-specific

claim: Federal law generally prohibits intentional interception subject to stated exceptions, including a participant-consent provision limited by criminal or tortious purpose
limitations: Does not establish that one participant's consent is sufficient under every applicable state law

claim: Federal law provides a civil action and remedies for qualifying violations
limitations: Availability and amount are claim-specific

claim: Meeting-capture review must separately address protected concerted activity and collective bargaining rather than treating recording consent as complete workplace authority
limitations: Coverage and current decisional law require qualified fact-specific review

claim: The NLRB General Counsel announced a 2025 position that secret recording of collective-bargaining sessions should be treated as a per se NLRA violation
limitations: Enforcement position is not a Board holding; verify later history

claim: Covered Title II and III entities must provide effective communication and may need auxiliary aids or services selected through a context-sensitive process
pinpoint: effective communication; auxiliary aids; primary consideration
limitations: An automated transcript is not presumed to satisfy the obligation

claim: GDPR analysis may require lawful-basis, transparency, rights, processor, security, impact-assessment, and Chapter V transfer review for a cross-border meeting-capture data flow
limitations: Territorial scope and the applicable mechanism must be determined for the actual parties and flows

claim: No jurisdiction row is cleared merely because federal and cross-border overlays have been registered
limitations: Each row requires current jurisdiction-specific authority and implicated-layer review

claim: Hawaii defines interception as acquisition through a device and limits oral communication to utterances made with a justified expectation against interception
limitations: Classification remains communication- and circumstance-specific

claim: For a person not acting under color of law Hawaii's statute generally permits interception when that person is a party or one party gave prior consent subject to the criminal-or-tortious-purpose limitation
limitations: Does not authorize every meeting later use multistate recording or conduct constrained by another legal layer

claim: An intentional interception outside an exception is a class C felony and qualifying violations may support substantial civil and equitable remedies
limitations: Liability remedy and defenses are fact-specific

claim: Hawaii's express constitutional privacy provisions and recent participant-recording decisions require the statutory result to remain bounded rather than treated as universal organizational authority
pinpoint: Haw. Const. art. I §§ 6-7; Aquino-Martinez pp. 3-5
limitations: Constitutional state-action analysis and nonprecedential law-enforcement facts do not complete private workplace privacy or later-processing review

claim: California Penal Code section 632 prohibits intentional recording of a confidential communication without consent of all parties and defines confidentiality by circumstances reasonably indicating a desire that the communication be confined to the parties
limitations: Public proceedings and circumstances where parties reasonably expect overhearing or recording are excluded; consent and confidentiality remain fact-specific

claim: California Penal Code section 632.7 separately requires all-party consent for intentional recording of covered communications involving cellular or cordless telephones and applies to participant recorders as well as nonparties
limitations: Device path exceptions and consent proof remain specific; Smith did not decide whether a beep plus continued participation established consent

claim: California provides statutory civil damages and injunctive relief for specified CIPA violations
limitations: Standing violation amount defenses and later statutory history remain claim-specific

claim: California choice-of-law analysis can apply its recording protections to interstate business calls involving a person in California while requiring a fact-specific comparative-impairment analysis
limitations: Kearney does not establish automatic California coverage for every multistate meeting or authorize recording after notice without actual consent analysis

claim: Massachusetts defines interception around secretly hearing or secretly recording a wire or oral communication without prior authority from all parties and criminalizes willful interception outside stated exceptions
limitations: Secrecy device scope prior authority statutory exceptions and First Amendment limits remain fact-specific

claim: Under the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court interpretation a recording made with actual knowledge of the recorded party is not secret and therefore is not an interception even without affirmative authorization or consent
limitations: Actual knowledge remains a fact question; assumed identity did not make the known recording secret but does not validate other deception or later processing

claim: Massachusetts separately penalizes knowing disclosure or use of communications obtained through an unlawful interception
limitations: Requires proof of unlawful interception knowledge use or disclosure and applicable defenses

claim: The First Circuit held section 99 unconstitutional only insofar as it prohibits secret nonconsensual audio recording of police officers discharging official duties in public spaces while rejecting a facial overbreadth challenge and leaving broader challenges unresolved
limitations: Narrow First Amendment holding does not clear workplace meetings private persons other officials nonpublic settings interference or later processing

claim: New York defines wiretapping as nonparty recording of a telephonic or telegraphic communication without consent of a sender or receiver and mechanical overhearing as nonpresent recording without consent of at least one party
limitations: Communication type recorder participation presence consent device and statutory authorization remain fact-specific

claim: New York makes unlawful wiretapping mechanical overhearing and electronic-communication interception or access a class E felony
limitations: The offense requires the statutory definitions unlawfulness and actual conduct; this does not authorize later processing or disclosure

claim: New York CPLR 4506 generally excludes communications and derivative evidence obtained through conduct constituting criminal eavesdropping and provides a civil suppression procedure for an aggrieved person
limitations: Crime predicate aggrieved-person status forum timing warrant and statutory exception remain proceeding-specific

claim: A New York participant may record a telephone conversation under New York law but an interstate call can require choice-of-law analysis and application of another state's stricter protections
limitations: Locke's California/New York civil facts do not establish which law governs every multistate meeting

claim: New Jersey defines interception as acquisition through a device and limits oral communication to speech carrying a justified expectation against interception
limitations: Communication type device use contemporaneous acquisition and expectation remain fact-specific

claim: New Jersey generally prohibits purposeful interception and knowing disclosure or use of unlawfully obtained communications outside statutory authority and grades a violation as a third-degree crime
limitations: Purpose knowledge statutory exceptions conduct and offense treatment require packet-specific analysis

claim: For a private person New Jersey generally permits interception when the person is a party or one party gave prior consent subject to criminal tortious or other injurious-purpose limits
limitations: Does not authorize every meeting later processing disclosure workplace monitoring or conduct governed by another jurisdiction or legal layer

claim: New Jersey provides a civil cause of action and actual or liquidated damages punitive damages fees and costs for qualifying unlawful interception disclosure or use
limitations: Liability standing damages causation defenses and later statutory history remain claim-specific

claim: New Jersey appellate analysis treats a justified expectation against interception as part of oral-communication coverage and rejected a Wiretap Act claim on the specific workplace facts before it
limitations: Stark is unpublished and fact-specific; it does not create general workplace authority or resolve notice consent labor privacy or later processing

claim: Florida limits protected oral communication to speech uttered with an expectation against interception under circumstances justifying that expectation and excludes public oral communication at a public meeting
limitations: Communication type device acquisition subjective expectation and objective justification remain fact-specific

claim: Florida generally prohibits intentional interception disclosure and use outside statutory authority and permits a private interception under the stated exception when all parties gave prior consent
limitations: Consent proof communication classification exceptions later use location and other applicable law remain packet-specific

claim: Florida separately makes interception for the purpose of committing a criminal act unlawful and provides criminal grading for qualifying violations
limitations: Purpose offense elements exceptions grading and actual conduct require qualified fact-specific analysis

claim: Florida provides a civil cause of action and equitable actual-or-liquidated punitive fee and cost remedies for qualifying unlawful interception disclosure or use while Florida Supreme Court precedent treats protected expectation as circumstance-specific
limitations: Claim accrual defenses damages and expectation evidence remain case-specific; opinion reproduction must be checked against official later history
